p.span: This part of the project will proceed largely in accordance with a plan for the inventory and stabilization of the tablets on loan to the Penn Museum from Iraq prepared by Museum staff in 2018; the presentation here is based on the one-page executive summary of that plan.

The work will be a collaboration between the Penn Museum and the Iraqi State Board of Antiquities and Heritage (SBAH). Iraqi partners, some of them conservators with experience in treating cuneiform tablets, others who are collections managers, will come to the Penn Museum in 6–8-week stints. The visits will be arranged in accordance with the preferences of SBAH.

will include consultation and partnership with SBAH as well as close collaboration between the Babylonian Section and the Registrar's office. During the condition assessment, we will need guidance on treatment priority and decision-making to determine whether fragments in poor condition will benefit sufficiently from time-intensive treatment. This will need to be established at the outset of the project and
will assist in determining how many tablets need treatment and the level of treatment needed before they can safely travel.

The budget for this work includes equipment costs in year 1 to ensure that the workspace meets requirements, as well as a dedicated camera set-up and supplies for treatment and packing (the packing accounts for the increase in supply costs in year 3). The camera set-up would also be used for photographing the published Ur III tablets from Ur which remain at the Penn Museum.

The Ur fragments are tracked by lot numbers SAM 1930-1-1 through SAM 1930-1-13 with each lot number referring to a tray of multiple tablets [SAM lots are unaccessioned batches of excavated material assigned a tracking number (SAM number) for Museum record keeping].

p: Each tray will be examined, and the tablets assigned an individual number based on their current SAM lots.

The tablets will be photographed in batches with the assigned numbers as a visual guide with at least two views of each tablet (front/back). These images may also serve as before treatment documentation for Phase 2. Some initial stabilization may be needed to move some of the tablets. These can either be flagged to evaluate with the Iraqi representative or blanket permission for some stabilization of the tablets should be sought.

The condition of each tablet will be assessed and recorded in a spreadsheet so that each tablet can be assigned a treatment category based on those condition issues. The spreadsheet will be created ahead of time and be provided along with a visual glossary to facilitate standard evaluation of condition issues.
Tablets will be re-housed to improve storage conditions and facilitate further work.

p.span: Treatments will be based on those recommended by the Iraqi partners with some modification likely based on available resources and supplies. This phase should begin after some of the condition assessment is completed, though overlap is possible depending on resource allocation and space. The Penn Museum’s project conservator will facilitate this project to ensure that all supplies are in place for the Iraqi partner, to work with them in treatment and protocol development and will continue to work between visits from Iraqi partners to ensure the steady progress of the conservation program. After treatment photo documentation of each tablet will be conducted by the project conservator or by a conservation technician.
